Embrace the role of an Inquisitor in the grim darkness of the not so far away future

Oh shit, that's not too far away. Terrifyingly, that last sentence is now a thing I can accurately write about games coming out in January 2027. Warhammer 40,000: Dark Heresy has just been confirmed as one such game, with the cRPG's heresy investigation set to commence towards the end of the month.

January 28th, 2027, is the full Dark Heresy release date, as announced by devs Owlcat on Steam. The beta version of the game'll be closing down on January 7th to make way for the full game, so as of writing there's still some time to give that a go if you fancy.

If this is the first you've heard of Dark Heresy, here's Owlcat's synopsis of what it's all about:

Embrace the role of an Inquisitor in the grim darkness of the far future in a cRPG set in the rich Warhammer 40,000 universe. Start your service as an acolyte of the Inquisition: Investigate heresy, command a diverse warband, and shape the fate of the Calixis Sector in a story-rich experience where every decision has weight, justice is non-existent, and the line between salvation and damnation is razor-thin. Explore an in-depth depiction of the Inquisition as an organisation and the vast force it commands: its power, bureaucracy, and inner conflicts laid bare like never before.

As an Inquisitor, you have one primary goal: to protect the Imperium, whether that be from the taint of xenos, the betrayal of heretics, or the scourge of mutants, by any means necessary. Be the conduit of the Emperor’s will in a place where all hope was lost decades ago, explore the mysteries of the maddening Tyrant Star, and overcome the worst horrors thrown at you by the Noctis Aeterna.

A place where all hope was lost decades ago? You sure this is the Warhammerverse and not real life lads? I jest, but bursting into rooms and shouting 'Nobody expects the God-Emperor’s inquisition!' Monty Python-style does sound quite fun. Oisin's previously written in more depth about what Dark Heresy devs have said regarding what to expect from its investigations, if you want nitty-gritty details rather than references to sketch comedy.

#3882. Ocarina of Time remake datamine suggests Master Quest is on the way

Ocarina of Time's notoriously tricky Master Quest mode could be making a comeback in the new remake.

Dataminer MrCheeze shared a list of strings from the remake's files on Bluesky, several of which tie the tag "MQ" to dungeons like Dodongo's Cavern.

In a follow-up, as spotted by TheGamer, they pointed to further entries, including "HasMQ", "IsMQModeExist", "NewGameMQ", and "ReleaseMQ".

Fellow dataminer OatmealDome added on Twitter/X that the mode will be unlocked by owning DLC, rather than arriving in an update, though "the data is incomplete". "I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly)," they said.

If you've not played it, Master Quest is a remixed version of Ocarina of Time with rearranged dungeons and tougher puzzles. It first appeared as a bonus disc on GameCube, then came back in 2011's Ocarina of Time 3D, which unlocked it after you finished the main game. That version also mirrored the whole world, which matches what OatmealDome has found, and had enemies deal double damage.

[Ocarina of Time] #ootspoilersThere is data in the game files for Master Quest. It will be unlocked by *owning DLC* - it is not just an update.The data is incomplete, but I can confirm that the world is mirrored and dungeons are modified (e.g. cows in Jabu-Jabu's Belly).

As with any datamine, there's no guarantee it'll ever see the light of day. Nintendo hasn't announced any DLC for the remake, and it's not clear whether Master Quest would be free, like it was on 3DS, or paid.

The Ocarina of Time remake launched on Switch 2 on 5th November. Donlan called the new version an "astonishing remake" in his five-star Eurogamer Ocarina of Time review.

The game's original worlds keep going from strength to strength

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

MTG Nauctis feels like it's going to repeat history, but in a good way. While Magic: The Gathering's approach to crossovers has met with mixed results, I don't think anyone could argue that its original IP has let the side down in 2026 – and based on everything we've seen so far of the underwater set from MagicCon Atlanta, it should continue that trend into next year.

MTG Nauctis is the first Magic release of 2027, and it's a new, entirely original world set beneath the waves. This is a planet completely covered by ocean, so it's split into distinct zones like the shallows and the dark Abyss, where temperatures fall and pressure is unforgiving. That means it's home to a host of underwater civilizations where Magic: The Gathering's team's creativity is allowed to go wild. However, this is one of the best card games, so it's also the source of fascinating new mechanics.

MTG Nauctis is Magic's first purely underwater set, and it's due to launch on February 5, 2027. It's made up of the usual booster sets, bundles, and four Commander decks. These are all up to pre-order at Amazon.

So much of this is tied to the set's underwater aesthetic. Judging by MTG's own explainer, its magic is heavily tied to the water; air can apparently trap foes or distort vision, for example. Tides may be able to speed your creatures along, and algae can heal or hinder. We don't have in-game examples of these yet, but Magic's own explainer provides a good idea of how it'll all work.

Personally, the thing that fascinates me most is the deeply layered worldbuilding at play here. Besides an entire world of underwater societies like mermaids, sharkfolk, and sea otters (here called 'Pinneons', a species of master artisans who can go between surface and sea), there are also hints at a compelling lost history. For instance, there are humans on Nauctis… and they claim that dry land once existed here, but was lost for reasons unknown. Now they make do as best they can on stilt cities, ships, and submarines that ply the ocean for scavenged goods.

It's one hell of a setup, and I'm already locked in – I can't wait to dive in come February.

#3879. Don't be fooled by Horses of Hoofprint Bay's hand-drawn art, this stable management game has all the drama of a Jilly Cooper novel

Poema is my pride and joy. She was my first horse and she's a competition winner, but she's reached her potential. She'll never be a show jumper, and that's where the money and prestige are to be found. If I'm ever to grow my horse farm into a nationally renowned equestrian centre, I need the cash to expand and upgrade my facilities. Poema is a hoofstep on the path to that future, but she's not going to be able to take me all the way herself.

For all its hand-drawn aesthetics, Horses of Hoofprint Bay has hard realities like the limits of Poema's future bubbling under its surface. While the game's scripted narrative may be lacking, it's shockingly easy to fill in the gaps with drama worthy of a Jilly Cooper novel.

There may be better author comparisons, but I learned everything I know about showjumping from Cooper's Riders – much as I learned everything about independent television franchise bids in the '80s from its sequel Rivals – a book which is as much about the nitty gritty of horsetraining and competing as it is about toffs jumping into bed with one another. In my mind the two are tightly connected - showjumping and Jilly Cooper, not horses and toff bonking. In Horses of Hoofprint Bay, the only real story you get is the fact you've scrimped and saved to buy your first horse and your uncle has lent you the use of his field while you start your business. I was hoping there would at least be a similar setup to Regency Solitaire, where your motivation for touring the country's tearooms is motivated by paying off your brother's gambling debts. Yet, despite this disappointing start, I soon found its business simulation mechanics provide great storytelling material.

Horses of Hoofprint Bay has many of the trappings of a cosy game. At the start of each day, you'll prepare the stables, dragging a rake around the yard to sling away the manure, clicking buckets of water to refill the trough, and making sure there's enough hay for all the horses. But this isn't just for the larks, if you skip these tasks there are serious knock on effects for yours horses. Forget to brush down your horses' coats or pick out the stones in their shoes, and they're liable to develop saddle sores and other injuries when you ride them. Leave an abrasion untreated and it can develop into an infection. Even something like taking a dirty horse to a contest can cost you. I forgot to brush Poema before entering her into her first contest and despite taking first place, her embarrassingly unkempt coat lost my stable prestige. It was a cruel end to what should have been a great celebration.

So long as your horses are well rested, you can train them each day. You may want to take them through some confidence building lunges, where they need to walk, trot, and canter on demand, or a more physically demanding Cavaletti or showjumping course. These latter too are much more tiring, but they build a horse's strength and endurance. The higher its endurance the more energy it can expend on training sessions each day, and the higher its strength the more jumps it can do in succession before slowing to a walk for a breather - essential when you're competing in a timed competition. Overdo the exercise, however, and you'll exhaust a horse, severely reducing its energy for the next day.

Now, unlike Poema, my freshly bought stallion Kolizey has the potential to compete in showjumping competitions. He'll never go all the way to the big national contests, but he can take a ribbon in the district and regional contests. Or he will when he's up to standard; he's arrived from the breeder in a sorry state: brambles in his mane, mud on his flanks, stones in his shoes, and his strength and endurance are far too low to make it through an entire course of obstacles.

The biggest problem, however, is Kolizey's confidence: it's shot. I don't know what was happening in the stalls at the breeder's, but he arrived at my stables backing up at the first sign of a jump. Before I can hope to earn him his first ribbon, I have to build up our relationship. If we exercise together enough in the yard, his confidence will grow and he will follow my direction without question.

It may be getting ahead of myself, but I also have plans for Kolizey and Poema to produce a foal. Done right, the two should raise a horse that's able to exceed its parents' potential, becoming stronger and more endurant than both of them. A stronger horse means a ticket to the bigger contests and the bigger prize pots. Not that I can start breeding the two just yet. I want both horses to be at peak physical fitness. Poema's already there, while Kolizey can't even manage a jump without shying away.

While getting Koliszey contest ready, I still need to be bringing in cash. That means using Poema as a training horse for students' riding lessons. The better I am at the minigame where I use the Q, E, W, A, S, and D keys to tell them to sit forward or back, hold the reins higher or lower, or to level out their legs, the more they tip me. I have to be careful, because when Poema is working with students, she's not being stretched, and her strength and endurance can wither which means she struggles to maintain her winning streak in the contests.

Another reason to hold off on getting Poema pregnant is that during the second half of her pregnancy, she can't be ridden, which means no contests and no lessons for students. Currently, those are my two main sources of income besides what I'm paid in rent to board a couple of nearby farmers' horses. I don't want her out of the rota when Kolizey isn't yet ready to step into her place.

And, well, while I'm on the subject of plans, reader, I must tell you, the future lies in semen. If I can build the facilities, earn the cash, and raise Kolizey's profile, I can make a good buck on his virile stallion cream. With the money I bring in from a prizewinning semen I can expand into the far field, creating space to take on more horses, upgrade my home from the caravan I'm living in currently, maybe even build a proper training school. I'm not going to afford all that by giving riding lessons to the local children or boarders' rent. No, the big money comes from competition wins and valuable horse sauce.

While Poema continues entering contests and carrying students, I start pushing Kolizey harder. Multiple training sessions every day. I begin with Cavaletti, which is a kind of obedience competition. Your horse has to be travelling at the correct speed when it passes marker flags – walking, trotting, or cantering – and make some small jumps over cross bars. It should be straightforward, but because Kolizey's confidence is so low, he keeps refusing my orders and trying to change speed. He warns me before he's about to speed up or slow down, and if I counter it in time he will obey me and even receive a little confidence boost, but often he does it just before a jump, messing up my timing and he hits the bars. Each time he fails a jump it knocks his confidence, risking me taking me even further from where I need him to be.

I try the easier lunges sessions. And they raise his confidence a little but they're doing little for his physical health. It's all taking too long and Poema's getting older every day. In a fit of frustration, and in mark that I may not be able to cut it as an animal trainer, I skip from the Cavaletti training straight into a showjumping qualifier. The time limits on these are much stricter, so you have to clear the course at a gallop. This is also where a horse's strength really comes into play. The faster you're going, the more strength it requires to jump an obstacle. Horses only recover strength when moving at a walk, so you don't want to tire a horse out by going at a gallop through the whole course, else they won't have the strength to make all the jumps and they'll be forced to withdraw from the event. But nor do you want to go too slowly and fall foul of the time limit.

I realise my mistake as soon as the course begins: I try to stir Kolizey into a walk he refuses. Thankfully the timer only starts when he crosses the line, but it's an inauspicious start. I tap forward again and he begins to walk. I tap again and Kolizey moves up to a trot, then to a canter, before picking up to a gallop. I think he's going too fast as we approach the first jump, but Kolizey clears it. Then another jump and another. With a nervous eye on the depleting strength bar, I tap him down to a canter for the next jump. We're halfway through the course, I briefly slow to a walk to recover some strength then take the next three jumps at a canter. We're so close to the end now but a big yellow exclamation mark appears next to the strength bar. Kolizey is on the edge of exhaustion but he refuses to slow down and increases to a gallop for the last two jumps.

He completes the course with a perfect clear. Not a single obstacle clipped and we end with ten seconds left on the timer. Not only has Kolizey earned his showjumping license, his success swells his confidence. He's a natural athlete.

The next day, with my horses rested, I take Kolizey and Poema to town to compete in the showjumping and Caprilli events respectively. They both bring home first place, raising the prestige of my stables, earning me a tidy little packet, and convincing me it's time my prized horses started a family. I'm perhaps too eager, when I try to send them to the breeding station, I'm told they're both 'Done for the day'. I suppose I should give my contest winners a bit of a break. They've earned it. I groom them and send them both to bed with an apple as a treat.

Except, maybe they weren't too tired: the next morning, I'm met with a message telling me Poema is pregnant. My stable's become the Olympic Village, with my rosette-winning horses working out the highs and stresses of competition in the only way they know how. Good on them. I needn't have even made the breeding station.

Then, with horror, I remember the horses I'm boarding for the neighbours. They're both stallions themselves. Neither of them are at competition level, their strength and endurance is lower even than Poema's when she arrived at the stable. If either of them are the father, Poema is about to be out of action for a whole season and at the other end of it I'll have a foal that can't even compete in the beginner events. fetch the equestrian version of Hercule Poirot, I need to find out who impregnated my horse!

It may not be a plot worthy of Cooper, but it will do for me.

#3878. COD: Modern Warfare 4 gets a surprisingly sudden free trial, so you can see what the game's extraction mode DMZ is like

Activision has released the first trial for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's extraction mode DMZ. The trial is available across PC (Steam / Battlenet), PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S until Wednesday, 11th November.

The free trial only includes access to DMZ and no other part of Modern Warfare 4, such as multiplayer or the campaign. And while it's not uncommon for Call of Duty titles to make some of their modes available for free for a limited time, the timing of this DMZ taster is notable.

DMZ launched days before Modern Warfare 4's 23rd October release date, meaning this first trial has arrived just two weeks after the game's full launch. By comparison, Black Ops 7's Endgame mode had its first free trial months after launch, in the game's third season. That said, Endgame continued to be freely available until Season 6.

The DMZ trial also coincides with the launch of Modern Warfare 4's iteration of free-to-play Call of Duty battle royale mode Warzone, and Season 1. Indeed, both DMZ and the new Warzone take place on the same Hajin map, so even if you don't decide to buy the full game to continue playing DMZ, some of that map knowledge will certainly transfer to Warzone.

The DMZ trial does not appear to have any limits, meaning you can climb the ranks, access Story Missions - the only way to play PvE, with caveats - and complete Orders to your heart's content. That includes X01, the new endgame dungeon-like area available to experienced and fully-equipped players.

DMZ players who've been asking Infinity Ward to offer a PvE-only playlist of the PvPvE mode will certainly be happy with the influx of new players, as they could potentially amplify their calls for a PvP-free playlist.

When World of Warcraft: Forever's beta first launched, I lamented its long stretches of silence and penchant for ambience over theatrics. I still sort of stand by that, but after spending more time in Azeroth (and discovering the loop music setting) I've a new-found appreciation for both WoW's soundtrack and ambient music as a whole.

It's also got me thinking about what makes a soundtrack ambient versus something more melodic. I'm chronically Final Fantasy 14-brained, where just about everything has a grand thematic soundtrack to it—the jauntiness of the Gold Saucer, the soothing Middle-earthness of Gridania's outer Shroud zones, the grand organs of Ishgard's bitterly cold landscape. You can't escape composer Masayoshi Soken's penchant for leifmotifs. He will turn anything into an orchestral spectacle.

I'm a big JRPG fan in general, a genre I think is the absolute master of thematic soundtracks. But I also think fondly of games I've played over the years that are a little more pared down, their soundtracks there for a little atmosphere rather than actively driving the narrative. Minecraft's OST is a masterclass in ambience, and is in regular rotation across my videogame-themed Spotify playlists. I also have a huge soft spot for the soundtrack behind Mirror's Edge—one which settles in this almost otherworldly ambiance, only ramping up when Faith is in a perilous situation.

But what about you? Do you prefer the more subtle nuances that an atmospheric soundtrack has to offer? Or do you like your videogame music loud, in your face, and full of dramatics? Be sure to leave a comment and let me know which one's your favourite and why.

#3875. GTA 6 reportedly has 55 Achievements/Trophies, more than both GTA 5 and Red Dead Redemption 2 had at launch

GTA 6 is due to release on the 19th November on PS5, and Xbox Series X/S, and ahead of the highly-anticipated launch of Rockstar's latest sandbox adventure, people just can't get enough information about the game. To that end, overnight, we saw our latest leak: the game will have 55 Trophies/Achievements.

In a now-deleted tweet from (in)famous Rockstar dataminer, TexFunz2 - re-posted by the Twitter account iGrandTheftAuto - it appears the game will have 55 individual rewards for completing certain tasks and missions. At the time of writing, we don't know specifically what these challenges are, but it seems none of them will be attached to the online version of the game; the base game launches without GTA Online, and so we can safely assume that all these rewards will be for the single-player only content. GTA Online will drop sometime in 2027, according to Twitch's CEO.

If you've been paying attention to previous Rockstar titles, you'll know that Grand Theft Auto 5 launched with 51 Achievements/Trophies - again, all single-player - and Red Dead Redemption 2 launched with 52. So the latest game has more than either game got at launch - and I can tell you from experience, getting Platinum in either title was a very time-consuming experience. Expect the same to be true here, too.

It's worth highlighting that GTA 5 did, eventually, get more Achievements and Trophies: the GTA Online content upped the complete total to 78, adding 27 new challenges to complete. I would expect GTA 6 to do the same… whenever the PC version of GTA comes out, or GTA Online lands in the new game (it's possible both could happen at the same time).

Recently, we heard why a former Rockstar Games tech director thinks GTA 6 could be coming to PC sooner than you'd expect (mostly thanks to AI clones), when we can expect the pre-load of the game (10th November), and how big the final game install is expected to be (210GB). The final game is expected to be so big and dense with detail that no single Rockstar employee has seen the entire game, meaning there are plenty of easter eggs and ridiculous things to discover.

#3874. Big Walk developer House House reveal genAI use in final stretch of development, only revealing it now as "it has become a matter of public interest"

Friendslop du jour Big Walk is the latest in an unfortunately long series of games that have been confirmed to use generative AI in their production, with developers House House clarifying their use of it in a statement to Aftermath (thanks!). House House state that "LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs", and that "well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage", but are quick to note that "generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

A specific example is given in the case of Unity's apparent weirdness around shadow casters in its rendering pipeline, as it's seemingly difficult to have unnecessary shadow casters behind the player culled, which resulted in the game running at half speed around sunrise and sunset. House House explain that they couldn't find a solution themselves, asked a Unity engineer for help who said it was impossible, and then decided the only answer was to ask an LLM chatbot; "after a few dead ends, it suggested a possible fix, and while we had to modify the suggestion extensively, it worked. This fix represented about 10 lines of code." While absolutely not the most pressing thing to mention here, it is very funny to me for House House to clarify that they "had to modify the suggestion extensively", almost as if this tech isn't actually helpful in giving useful answers.

So, House House touched the stove, despite how easy it is to simply not touch the stove. The thing is, this wasn't a case of being forced to by upper management, as is sometimes the case. This was a choice made entirely voluntarily, and House House are attempting to have their cake and eat it by ending their statement with the reflection that "We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as “inevitable”. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards." But then, you know, that's followed up by saying that Big Walk was developed "without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards." So, not to worry, they learned touching the stove is bad by touching the stove, and definitely won't do it again in future. If only there were thousands of other cases informing them why touching the stove is bad.

Very relevant to this reveal is the recent statement by select jurors of the Independent Games Festival which, after much internal deliberation, came to the conclusion that those who sign the statement would decline to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity, with signees including Austin Walker, Sam Barlow, Lena Reine, Brendon Chung, Aura Triolo, aurahack and more. The statement specifies that "AI-generated code is not an exception to these harms." Fellow juror Liz Ryerson confirmed that Big Walk was being considered by the IGF, and was a matter of discussion in judging as to whether its use of genAI would be acceptable.

As for House House only disclosing this now, they state it was not only because it was necessary for their IGF submission, but also that "we have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage", and that they have spoken on it publicly to Aftermath because "it has become a matter of public interest."

If I were to be cynical, I would say that House House would prefer to be the ones breaking this news themselves rather than having the IGF reveal that they had been hiding their use up until now; it's usually easier to control PR if you release it yourself. Big Walk had already been securely in everyone's good books for its support for the BDS boycott, for example, so why ruin that clean rep with something like a genAI disclosure?

I don't know how better to close this article than with an excerpt from that very IGF statement:

"We know that change does not come at the individual level, but as independent developers, we also know firsthand the value of pushing back on what an industry has deemed "inevitable." As jurists, we feel a responsibility to push past defeatism and aspire to a higher ideal.

The future is not yet settled. You are not alone. We can stand together."

#3873. 40th Anniversary Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks live: where to check for new waves of stock

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 restocks have remained dry over the last week, but more could be on the way shortly. Sites like Amazon and Nintendo have been drip-feeding new handhelds onto the shelves in smaller waves, while stores like Target and GameStop have prioritized in-store options instead.

That means the hunt for the special edition 40th Anniversary handheld marches on, and with the biggest shopping week of the year on the horizon it's likely we'll see a little more action here shortly. Thanksgiving week represents a massive opportunity for retailers to secure eyes on their holiday discounts by also dropping Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock at the same time.

Only time will tell if everyone is holding off for next week's Black Friday deals, if we spot a new listing or a sniff of stock anywhere across the US or UK, we're bringing it right here to you first.

I've been tracking hard-to-find stock for over six years now, starting with the incredibly limited releases of the PS5 and Xbox Series X. I've been reporting on how retailers operate with high-demand products, from anniversary releases to brand new consoles, ever since then - including the Nintendo Switch 2 itself.

Amazon has been restocking the Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 in bits and pieces for a little while now. Drops have dried up in recent days, but the little-and-often mantra has definitely been true here in the past.

Ocarina of Time (digital): $54.99 (was $59.99)

Walmart fumbled its pre-orders and hasn't dropped any Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks since. Now, the site seems to have removed its listing for the special edition handheld, with the Pro Controller and carry case either out of stock or monstrously price-inflated. Still, that could all change at any time.

Target ran its own Zelda Switch 2 restocks when Ocarina of Time remake first dropped. It's been quiet since then, though, without a word on when new handhelds or accessories will be available.

Best Buy has been similarly quiet since Ocarina of Time remake launched, opting for an in-person midnight event to celebrate the game (and hand out a few special edition consoles at the same time).

Nintendo itself seems to be one of the more reliable retailers out there. The brand's own store page has been dropping small amounts of handhelds every now and then over the last week, so it's well worth keeping in touch.

GameStop is only running Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 restocks in stores, so you won't find any online stock here. The store looks like it's about to start running Pro Controller and carry case restocks online, though.

Amazon UK has been a pretty reliable source of Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks in the last few weeks, even if things have slowed down in recent days. Like its US counterpart, the site is dropping a small number of special edition handhelds at a time.

EE has had two Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks since launch day, but the boost here comes from those bundles. The site has previously been offering discounts on Ocarina of Time remake and Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream when bought with the device.

Smyths Toys has seemingly removed its Legend of Zelda Switch 2 listing, which is odd for one of the few UK retailers with the whole collection previously on its site. The Pro Controller page is still up, even if the carry case has also mysteriously vanished here.

Here's the thing with Very. It often bundles up difficult-to-find stock with extra accessories or games to keep resellers at bay. That means you'll be paying a little more here (though still only RRP for everything you're getting) but stock often holds out a lot longer.

Argos was previously offering Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock ahead of launch, but things look to have run dry now. The store organises its inventory by postcode, though, so it's always worth checking your local area's delivery and collection options.

Currys previously had a listing page up for the Legend of Zelda Switch 2, but it seems to have disappeared now, instead sending us to a generic consoles search page.

Nintendo has also stated more stock is on the way, so you'd expect its own store to be one of the first with fresh handhelds up for grabs.

Very is currently bundling its Legend of Zelda Switch 2s with Ocarina of Time (well it would be if stock was live). Still, that means it's likely these will be a little easier to get hold of when availability drops once again. You're not saving any money on the game itself (unlike EE's supplies), but packaging the game in from the off often deters resellers long enough for actual fans to get to checkout.

Target gave us a fair warning last time it restocked the Legend of Zelda Switch 2. The retailer announced its November 5 and November 6 drops right on the listing page itself. Right now, though, it looks like the store doesn't have anything in the works - at least nothing it wants to shout about just yet.

A jumpscare of Amazon stock just flitted across my screen, but it looks like this is the return of the £499.99 price we were seeing ahead of launch. The Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 is technically available at the retailer, but it should be noted that the handheld itself carries a £429.99 price tag when sold by reputable sellers. Avoid this one.

Walmart's Legend of Zelda Switch 2 listing page has been out of commission for just over a week now, with no sign of returning. The retailer's mishandling of its pre-orders were originally to blame for its lack of stock, as the store sought to catch up on mistakenly cancelled orders. However, with radio silence and not even a picture of the handheld on the site, things are looking squeaky here.

UK Legend of Zelda stock hunters should be keeping in touch with Argos when new shipments arrive. Competition is significantly lower here - the retailer runs its restocks through local inventory. That means you're only up against those in your local area when new handhelds are available.

GameStop isn't running online Zelda Switch 2 restocks, instead sending customers to their brick and mortar stores. It's well worth checking in with your local, though, stock levels are going to be different across the country and we don't know when those fresh shipments are due in.

EE has been running an additional promotion around its Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock in the last few weeks. Consoles are available with £10 off the Ocarina of Time remake, £21.49 off Pokemon Pokopia, or £22.08 off Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. While stock is still currently unavailable, EE has been one of the more active retailers in the last few weeks.

The Zelda Switch 2 restock pattern we're seeing at the moment rewards those in the right place at the right time. Retailers are dropping very small amounts of stock irregularly, so those 'Add to cart' buttons can jump to life at any moment, and die just as quickly. That's why it's so important to make sure you stay signed into retailer accounts throughout your stock hunt.

Getting through to checkout as quickly as possible is the real challenge here, and any clicks you can save signing in, filling out delivery information, and adding payment details can see you fall behind the pack.

The reseller market is rife with inflated prices this week and marketplace sellers are starting to lift those costs on larger retailers as well. That's why it pays to know exactly how much you should be paying for 40th Anniversary Legend of Zelda kit:

While stock itself is still nowhere to be found, GameStop looks like it's opened up the possibility of online Zelda Switch 2 Pro Controller and carry case restocks. The handheld itself is still strictly in-store, but those accessories are listed as 'Coming Soon' or 'Currently Unavailable' online, rather than pointing customers towards their local stores.

Nintendo itself has been one of the more reliable retailers this restock period, and while it's been a little quieter as of late it is running a notification system. Head over to the official Legend of Zelda Switch 2 listing and you'll find a link to the Nintendo Store app. As long as you're signed in, you can add the handheld to your wish list and you'll be notified next time stock drops onto the shelves.

Legend of Zelda Switch 2 | Check stock at Nintendo

Walmart's listings also include third party marketplace sellers, and this is where we often see inflated prices on hard-to-find gadgets. It's happening with the Zelda Pro Controller and has been spotted on the carry case and handheld as well.

This is just a reminder not to pay over MSRP for your Legend of Zelda kit, but to also filter your Walmart search results to those only sold by Walmart itself.

With such a quiet week last week, it makes sense to expect a fresh wave of Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks shortly. Retailers have had another week to fill their warehouses now, so it makes sense that those handhelds will be filing onto the shelves soon.

It could be this week, but it's more likely that next week is going to be the big one. With Black Friday nearly upon us, stores are going to want to go bigger at the end of the month.

#3872. Dungeons in World of Warcraft: Forever get a huge XP buff, but power-levellers shouldn't celebrate just yet

World of Warcraft: Forever has received a massive buff to the XP drop-rates of dungeon mobs (enemies), which should make running these instances multiple times feel more rewarding - and may revive an older levelling strategy.

This buff is a 50 percent increase in experience from all mobs killed inside all dungeons. As detailed in this World of Warcraft forum post, community manager Kaivax wrote that this change has been made "so it feels better to go back in for more runs". They don't outright say this is in response to community feedback, but the subject has been a hot topic since the beta.

World of Warcraft: Forever developers have spoken in the past about the decision to deliberately bring down dungeon mob XP to disincentivise power-levelling in dungeons. The idea was that by doing this, people would be encouraged to actually go out into the world and explore it, rather than hopping from instance to instance until they reached max level.

Sadly, a side effect of this change is that doing a dungeon more than once could feel unrewarding. Playing it once is great, as you get to complete lots of quests that reward guaranteed items and XP. However, if you go back again, you don't get these, so your only source of progression comes from a heavily decreased XP rate.

Some quests exacerbate this issue. Dungeons like Wailing Caverns and especially Blackfathom Deeps have a quest that can't really be completed in one run due to a reliance on drop rates for items you need, and having to fight for drops with the rest of your dungeon party. Having to go back to complete this used to suck, and now it sucks less!

So does this mean farming dungeons to power-level is back? Maybe, but it still won't be nearly as efficient as it was in older versions of Classic WoW. The current mob XP rates, after this buff, will still only be 36 percent of the original Classic rate - a third. Given how fast you can level by doing quests out in the world, it seems dungeon farming isn't due for a comeback just yet.

After an especially smooth launch, World of Warcraft: Forever has become the biggest launch in the series' history, beating out Wrath of the Lich King, Cataclysm, and all the other past expansion launches. The developers have been quick to hotfix things on the fly, including a change that left PvP battlegrounds heavily advantaged for the Horde.

#3871. Following site-wide discussion on AI use, Nexus Mods add a "daily limit" to the spots in the new mods tab one person can hog via multiple rapid-fire uploads

It's a "stopgap solution" while the site's staff are busy "working on more sophisticated tools"

The folks behind Nexus Mods have rolled out a new "daily limit" system which ensures modders who upload multiple works in bulk during a single 24 hour period can't take up more than one spot in the tabs dedicated to showing off new mods for different games. Instead, those who chuck up their mods in bulk will see one of their works given a spot, while the rest are neatly filed away behind it, ready to spring out if you click a bit of text indicating that modder's got other fresh works to show off.

"Nexus Mods owner and CEO Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann hinted measures related to making the glut of new mods currently uploaded on a daily basis less of a discovery nightmare in last week's announcement post about the site's current policy regarding the use of genAI in mod making. "We’ve received feedback regarding authors uploading numerous mods at once and overwhelming the Recently Added section, pushing everyone else down the page," he wrote. "This is less of an issue related to AI, but it’s becoming much more prevalent as mod production is speeding up. Thus, we’re trying out limits on the number of mods from one author that can be shown in this section to give others a better chance of getting noticed. We’re also putting tighter restrictions on uploads from newly created accounts. The first of these updates will be available soon."

Cue an an announcement on Nexus Mods' Discord server yesterday by community manager Phoenix introducing the new "daily limit", which Nexus were keen to emphasise is "an experiment" they're open to feedback on. "We know that time in the New Mods view is important for a new mod to be discovered and we believe every mod author should have equal chances of having their work seen," they wrote. "While we're working on more sophisticated tools to give you control over the mods displayed to you, we are testing a stopgap solution that we hope will address the issue for now: For the time being, the New Mods view will display one mod per mod author. This limit refreshes every twenty-four hours – so if you publish one mod every day, you won't be affected."

The All Mods, Updated, Trending, Popular, and Surprise tabs for games are unaffected by the change, so will still dedicate a tab to each work regardless of who uploaded it when. If you take a glance at the New Mods pages for the likes of Skyrim, Fallout 4, and Cyberpunk 2077 this morning, you can already see the new mod stacking in action. The most mods from the same author I've seen stacked atop each other so far is 14 Fallout 4 works piled up.

It's worth noting you can also toggle the show only one new mod per modder rule off in the new mods tab, bringing back the older layout with one slot per mod regardless of uploader.

Personally, I tend to sort by mods with the most endorsements or downloads within the past 24 hours or seven days when I'm scanning for new mods, rather than just scrolling back through the new mods tab. Though I appreciate that could mean I've been missing out on some stellar works by lesser known modders whose creations never get the traction they merit thanks to being buried under an avalanche of other works. If so, hopefully this update does help the lone mods avoid being run over by mass upload freight trains.

#3870. Mercenaries Grace launches November 25 for PS5 in Japan, in December for Switch, and in early 2027 for PC

Strategy RPG Mercenaries Grace will launch for PlayStation 5 on November 25 in Japan for 3,850 yen, followed by Switch in December, and PC via Steam in early 2027, developer RideonJapan announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:

A young mercenary spreads his wings toward tomorrow! A tale of an iron prosthetic and an unwanted queen.

Mercenaries Grace is a tactical simulation RPG set in a fantasy world. Battles occur on quarter-view maps with height differences, where character positioning in the front, back, and side of enemy units may very well determine each battle’s outcome.

The Kingdom of Grauses has long suffered under the tyranny and crushing taxes of the Regent O’Neill. With his sudden death in battle, the citizens rejoiced, expecting the long-awaited coronation of the late king’s heir.

Meanwhile, a small unit attacks the “Forbidden Tower” located in a taboo land in the northern reaches of the kingdom. Among them are the “Iron Hand Mercenaries,” led by the young mercenary Swan—the right-hand man of the legendary iron-prosthetic-wielding leader, Garsh. From the depths of the Forbidden Tower, Swan and his comrades rescue the beautiful General Berta. However, she turns out to be the biological younger sister of the late Regent O’Neill.

Upon her release, Berta is pushed forward by O’Neill’s former loyalists to be crowned as the next queen. What chaos will be unleashed by this unlawful ascension, driven by corrupt ministers desperate to protect their own vested interests? And where will the hands of fate lead Swan and Berta?

Mercenaries Grace is a tactical simulation RPG set in a rich fantasy world.

Battles take place on quarter-view isometric maps with distinct elevation changes. Strategy is paramount: combat outcomes shift based on whether you attack from the front, back, or sides, and positioning allies correctly unlocks powerful support effects.

Use Skill Points earned in battle to learn and upgrade skills, change classes, and enjoy highly customizable character progression.

Featuring stunning character designs by illustrator mitsu_plus! Watch the beautifully drawn characters come to life with a rich array of emotional expressions.

While previous entries in the Mercenaries Saga series utilized a phase-based system where all player characters acted followed by all enemy characters, this title introduces a massive overhaul!

Combat now shifts to an alternate-turn system—similar to chess or shogi—where players and enemies take turns moving one character at a time. Predicting who to move next and anticipating the enemy’s sequence adds a whole new layer of depth to the battlefield.

The “Ladder Class” System: Eight Branching Paths

In previous titles, each character started in an initial class that split into two intermediate paths, eventually leading to advanced and special classes for a total of seven possibilities.

This game introduces the “Ladder Class” system, breaking past traditional boundaries like Warrior, Thief, Priest, and Mage into eight distinct lineages. As characters promote through Novice, Intermediate, Advanced, and Special tiers, they are not locked into a linear path—they can also cross over to adjacent class branches.

How you grow your characters as they climb the ranks is entirely up to you!

Midway through the story, a pivotal choice will cause the narrative to split drastically.

While previous entries changed story developments and recruitable allies based on your route, this game introduces completely unique “Awakening” systems for each path that temporarily power up your units. The “Awakening” command unlocks after progressing past a certain point in the story. Much like the “Soul Exceed” ultimate moves, it is activated by consuming accumulated power stocks.

What kind of power-ups await you on each path? Play and find out!

Engaging in combat fills a gauge in the top right corner of the screen. By consuming stocked power, characters can unleash their ultimate move: “Soul Exceed.”

These ultimate abilities vary by Ladder Class—ranging from dealing devastating damage to enemies to fully healing the party’s HP and removing status ailments.

Mastering these ultimate moves is the ultimate key to victory!

Battlefields are now rendered in full 3D models, allowing players to freely rotate the camera angle during their turn.

Changing your perspective might even reveal hidden items tucked away in the environment!

The options menu includes features perfect for replayability and grinding, such as toggling the 3D battle map grid ON/OFF, streamlining skill animations with “Simple Skill Effects,” and accelerating gameplay with “Fast Movement.”

Miniature designer and artist Aly Morrison has died, as confirmed by Trish Carden Miniatures and Design on Facebook. Carden, Morrison's ex-wife and former partner in Marauder Miniatures, posted that, "Mharaid and I are heartbroken to announce the passing of Aly Morrison, a very much loved father, veteran wargames miniatures designer and friend to many around the tabletop and the world. Aly passed unexpectedly but peacefully this Wednesday, and will be sorely missed."

Aly Morrison began sculpting for Citadel in 1983 as a freelancer before joining the studio full-time in 1986. He and Trish were then made stewards of Games Workshop's imprint Marauder Miniatures in 1988, where they had free reign to create quirky and characterful figures like the mohawked dwarf trollslayers and the giant with a whaler's beard and a booze barrel strapped to his waist that became archetypal parts of Warhammer.

Morrison also crafted the first miniatures for Blood Bowl players and drew the tokens to represent them in the board game's first edition. During his time at Games Workshop every faction from dark elves to space marines eventually benefited from his touch.

He's also well-regarded as a painter, and his reliance on a dark wash with a hint of purple in it jokingly known as "Aly's Brown Liquid" was legendary. He continued working on the recipe over the years, with a recent iteration described on his blog in 2020 if you want to whip some up yourself.

Though Marauder was eventually folded back into Citadel, Morrison continued at Games Workshop until his retirement earlier this year. The company remembered him by saying, "Aly’s kindness and generosity as a mentor have left an indelible mark on the Warhammer Studio. Humble, magnanimous and with an incorrigible wit, to sit beside Aly and hear his wisdom and love of Warhammer miniatures design, was to be in the presence of a master. No matter your level of experience, he always had something insightful to add, to help make the creation 'more Warhammer'."

Expensive British department store Selfridges has launched a sizeable Grand Theft Auto 6 takeover, completely making-over its Oxford Street London Corner Shop store and offering a considerable line of clothing, which includes an exclusive varsity jacket that costs a bank-melting £2,500. Note, you can buy the GTA 6 items online as well.

Live from Selfridges at Oxford Street for the #GTAVI activation🌴Rockstar are not messing around 🤯 pic.twitter.com/vqqXKwB1oJ

That GTA 6 varsity jacket is by far and away the most expensive item (and it's apparently already sold out), next to a non-exclusive varsity jacket that's £1,750, whereas the other items are pricey but conceivably affordable.

There are a few ranges on offer. There's a nice bright teal and pink-coloured range based around the spoof NFL team the Vice City Manatees, which includes a manatee plushie, an American football, a jacket, and other bits and bobs. There's also a range based around the spoof NBA team, the Vice City Narcos, that includes a basketball (there's a standard GTA 6-branded basketball too).

There's a range based on the spoof fast-food chain Burger Shot, which includes a visor, work uniform, and apron, amusingly. There are some admirably horrid postcard-decorated shirts and shorts, and there's a lot of generic game-branded caps and T-shirts besides, all in quite nice colours. Quirky branded offerings include an ashtray, money clip and dartboard. It's all quite attractive stuff.

There's no word on how long the items will be stocked for or that the Selfridges Corner Shop takeover will run for, other than "while stocks last".

#3867. Skydance Games lay off an undisclosed number of staff in the wake of Paramount-Warner Bros. merger, in latest case of consolidation killing livelihoods

A little over a month following the huge, vile, culture-defining (negative) merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. into Skydance, the corporation has confirmed that games division Skydance Games will be facing a round of layoffs, according to a report from Variety.

Skydance Games was born from combining Paramount and Warner Bros' own individual divisions, bringing developers like NetherRealm, Rocksteady, WB Games Montreal/Boston, TT Games and Avalanche under the same umbrella as Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra developers and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: The Last Ronin publishers Paramount Games Studio. All this was was done, of course, to maximise the amount of IP that the corporation can access to base games on, such as Avatar: The Last Airbender, Game of Thrones, Star Trek, the DC Universe, Harry Potter, and more. Skydance Games came into existence on October 6th; it barely lasted a month as it was.

In a statement given to Variety, Skydance confirmed that "As part of our ongoing efforts to position Skydance Games for long-term growth and success, we are implementing reorganization and operational shifts across a few areas of our business. We have stepped back and taken some time to consider where we are investing our efforts and have made the difficult decision to scale down some of our projects. As a result, there are roles impacted. This is not a reflection of the talent, dedication, or creativity of those affected and we are grateful for their contributions. We are committed to approaching the process with transparency, care and respect for those who are leaving the company." Skydance did not disclose the number of staff affected.

Skydance joins the ever-growing list of corporations that have mandated layoffs in the recent past, such as Microsoft, Ubisoft, and EA. Workers will bleed until there is no one left to cut. Solidarity to all affected.

The 30th D.I.C.E. awards will feature the presentation of the inaugural award

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Academy of Interactive Arts and Sciences (AIAS) has confirmed that Mario, Donkey Kong and The Legend of Zelda creator Shigeru Miyamoto will be the inaugural recipient of its new Legend Award.

AIAS – which runs the annual D.I.C.E. Awards – has confirmed that for the 30th edition of its award show it will introduce a new award, that being the Legend Award. This award is being treated as the most exclusive accolade AIAS can give, with it being described as a "generational honor," so much so that it will be presented only once per decade.

It's intended for "an industry icon whose enduring vision continues to redefine interactive entertainment. Honoring creators whose groundbreaking achievements have already earned lasting universal acclaim, this award also celebrates their immeasurable impact and influence that is still being felt in the work of game makers and entertainers in every entertainment medium today and well into our future," it's explained.

Meggan Scavio, president of the AIAS says in a press release, "Shigeru Miyamoto is widely recognized as one of the most respected and impactful figures in the games industry and beyond." She explains, "We believe he perfectly embodies our inaugural Legend Award through his impact and reach, and we are so humbled and excited to have Mr. Miyamoto accept this award at the 30th anniversary of the D.I.C.E. Awards."

I mean, really, who else could it have been? While the games industry has been built on the backs of millions of people over the years, it's hard to argue that anyone has had a singular impact more than Miyamoto… creating Mario alone would've guaranteed that. That's why it was also no surprise when just last month he became the first game developer to receive the Japanese Order of Culture in its almost 90-year history.

The real question is who will be receiving the award in 10 years' time. Miyamoto was an obvious first choice, but in at the 40th D.I.C.E awards, the likes of Hideo Kojima, Yoko Shimomura, Eiji Aonuma, Alexey Pajitnov, Roberta and Ken Williams, and a ton of other names who would be shoo-ins for an award like this.

Pachinko-inspired roguelike game High Roller Penny, a pachinko-inspired roguelike game, will launch for PC via Steam on January 12, 2027, developer Kniv Studio announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page:

High Roller Penny is a pachinko-inspired roguelike about creating big numbers for your freedom and the happiness of your Bunny Girl.

Drop a ball down your pegboard and watch it fly, with every peg hit adding points to your score. Overcome the quota, and you’ll live to see another round. But strike out, and you’re literally dead!

As the challenger, your goal is to defeat all other bunny girls and rise to the top of the ranks! If you win, Penny claims her glory and your debts are fully repaid. If you lose… well, it’s best not to think about it.

Either way, you don’t have much of a choice. Go big… or get executed on the spot!

#3864. "Art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI" Bandai Namco and Monolith Soft helped out with Ocarina of Time on Switch 2

Xenoblade series developer Monolith Soft and Bandai Namco Studios have been listed as support studios for the Switch 2 version of Ocarina of Time, working on elements of the title such as "art, including characters, terrain, animations, cutscenes and UI". Special thanks to both companies appear in the credits for the newly-launched game (as you can see below) and a statement released by Bandai Namco Studios confirms its involvement, too.

"We were commissioned to produce some of the visual assets and artwork, including characters, environments, animations, cutscenes, and UI elements, for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, a Nintendo Switch 2 game released by Nintendo Co., Ltd. on 5th November, 2026," reads a translated release from Bandai Namco Studio reads.

Of course, this isn't the first time we've seen Bandai Namco Studios' talents leveraged to help with Nintendo games: the publisher and its internal studios worked closely with Nintendo as a co-developer on the long-awaited Metroid Prime 4, and we know the studios are listed as co-developer for first-party Switch 2 titles like Mario Kart World and Splatoon Raiders. Typically, the work carried out by Bandai Namco comes from one of two dedicated internal studios that are contracted specifically to work with Nintendo: Studio 2 and Studio S. You can see a full list of the games Bandai Namco's support studios have worked on here. You'll note there are many Nintendo first-party titles listed here, going back to 2012 and Mario Kart 8. In late 2025, Nintendo acquired Bandai Namco Studios Singapore from the publisher, renaming the company Nintendo Studios Singapore.

"Alongside great judgement and clever tweaks, this astonishing remake has a proper ace up its sleeve," wrote our reviewer, Christian Donlan, in his five-star review of the Switch 2 game last week. "This is Ocarina as it's always been, as timeless and intricate, but it also has a vibrancy and clarity that makes it feel like it was just created last Wednesday."

If - somehow! - you've already gobbled up most of the game and you're keen to play it again, you will be pleased to know that Master Quest code has been found in datamined files for the title, suggesting DLC may well be on the way in the not-too-distant future.

#3863. Steam's new Steam Deck framerate graphs are good news for handheld players, though I wouldn't fully trust the numbers yet

Valve have finally made clear what they've been doing with all that hoovered-up performance data and all those "Framerate Estimator" text strings: a framerate estimator for the Steam Deck. Or, rather, a framerate average-r, as games on the Steam Store are now getting attached graphs – under their existing Steam Deck Compatibility details – that show how many frames-per-secondseses that game has been recording on real players' handhelds, the OLED and original LCD models both.

The thinking, as Valve explain in a Steam post, is to set more precise performance expectations than the existing verification ratings – Verified, Playable, and Unsupported – provide. This may induce some gentle learned nodding, if you've ever tried an Unsupported game only to find it works more or less fine, or have ever wondered why a game that can just about scrape 30fps together gets the same green good-job sticker as something that screams along at 90fps. Now, when checking that rating, you'll also get a relatively specific idea of smoothness and/or chugging potential.

Or will you? By Valve's own admission, the displayed results may be skewed by V-Sync treachery, where this anti-screen tear setting (which many games enable by default) could force games into briefly running at unrepresentative framerates. The scoundrel. My current handheld game beau, Mortal Shell II, looks like it may be falling victim to this: its results for the LCD Steam Deck show it mostly runs around 30fps, which is in line with my experience, but the OLED results show it averaging around 45fps. The Steam Deck OLED's APU is a tiny bit quicker than the LCD Deck's, but it's not that much of an upgrade.

There's work to be done, then, though I do appreciate the concept. As tightly as I cling to my battery-efficient, mercifully Windows-free Deck OLED in the face of drastically more powerful handhelds, with every year it becomes a little less likely that new games will comfortably run on it. Verification ratings can still act as decent (if broad) guidelines, but even with V-Sync putting an immaculately untorn thumb on the scales, game-specific framerate data will be much more illustrative.

As for whether these histograms will also get Steam Machine versions, or perhaps cover non-Valve handhelds, Valve say this: "We see this update as a stepping stone toward providing framerate data for more devices than just Steam Deck. To this end, we are also prompting customers to opt-in to providing anonymized framerate data in the Steam desktop client. This opt-in is currently only on Steam Client Beta, and will ship to all customers in the future." So, maybe, if you gizzus yer data.

The preview version of SteamOS 3.10.0 has just dropped, and with it comes better support for AMD and Nvidia hardware, and it's now based on Linux kernel 7.3.

For AMD graphics, the latest SteamOS update adds support for HDMI 2.1 VRR (Variable Refresh Rate), FRL(Fixed Rate Link), and ALLM (Auto Low Latency Mode). This should all contribute to a smoother gaming experience with higher bandwidth video and less input lag.

As for Nvidia graphics, it has reportedly received increased stability and performance, alongside support for Mesh Shaders on Turing and newer architectures. The latest SteamOS updates also fixed rendering corruption issues in Shadow of the Tomb Raider and The Surge 2.

Then, of course, SteamOS now uses the Linux 7.3 kernel (which launched last month).

Those are the big updates from SteamOS 3.10.0, but there are also a handful of fixes and changes. Game Mode has had the following changes:

SteamOS Previews are experimental by nature. You have to swap your update channel in Steam settings to get access, and there's always a chance new updates come with bugs or stability problems. If you come across a problem, Valve has a form to track SteamOS bugs.

If you don't fancy downloading a preview, SteamOS 3.10.0 is likely to come to the public channel at some point in the future, based on feedback from the preview.

#3861. Tripwire Interactive says it's laying off 36 staff in a "necessary" decision, while reassuring that Killing Floor 3 and Maneater 2 are still in active development

In a statement posted yesterday, Killing Floor developers Tripwire Interactive have announced that the studio is laying off 36 "talented" internal staff as part of a "workforce reduction". The job cuts come 16 months after the release of Killing Floor 3 (which James didn't care for), and within hours of unrelated yet equally dispiriting redunancies at Skydance Games.

Tripwire's announcement claims that this was "not an easy decision, but unfortunately a necessary one for the organisation," adding that "these are truly great people who are exceptional at their roles, and we will help support these individuals with compassion and dignity during this transition." There's a small hope in me that this might mean helping those affected find new jobs quickly, though it's hard to stay optimistic when mass layoffs in games development have become such a regular occurrence.

Despite this post primarily being about the loss of 36 livelihoods, Tripwire are quick to reassure fans that Killing Floor 3's post-launch updates remain in active development, as does their comedy shark-action sequel Maneater 2. The studio "remain committed to our awesome community", they say; apparently just not to their awesome employees.

This news also arrives just days after Tripwire expanded its publishing business to support small indie developers, and less than a year after its last round of layoffs in March. Tripwire also happens to have been acquired by layoff extraordinaire corporation Embracer in 2022, just for some relevant context.

#3860. Skyrim lead designer hopes Sentinel will finally solve The Elder Scrolls' ladder problem

For such a simple, straightforward real-world object, ladders have been the bane of game developers' existence since the early days of the industry. And Bethesda's The Elder Scrolls Series is certainly no stranger to that struggle.

While we may be years away from the release of The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel, the recent title reveal reignited conversations about what longtime fans hope to see from it. That includes former Bethesda developers, such as Skyrim lead designer and Bethesda veteran Bruce Nesmith, who picked ladders as one thing he hopes Sentinel actually figures out.

If you're unfamiliar, ladders in Skyrim work in a weird way. You don't animatedly climb up and down them, but rather the character simply teleports from one end to the other. Speaking to The Examined Game (via GamesRadar+), Nesmith said that Skyrim's approach "really limits the art team in terms of how you can do multi-layer [levels]".

"It seems simple, it seems stupid, but you don't climb up and down ladders," said Nesmith. "All the ladders in Skyrim, you click on the ladder, poof, you're at the top or you have to climb a stair.

"But to do ladders, you have to deal with a whole host of questions which our programmers very legitimately put in front of us and said, 'You give me answers to these, I'll tell you how much programming time it's going to take to make them.' And you know, that caused problems right there."

Nesmith then pointed out the hidden complexity of creating functioning ladders in games, and the scenarios developers have to anticipate and account for, especially in a game as dynamic as an Elder Scrolls title.

"So, I'm halfway up a ladder, and [an] NPC decides to climb down it. What happens?" Nesmith posited. "The NPC has to have AI that will adjust for that. Does the player go through the NPC? Is he blocked by the NPC? Does the NPC stay on the ladder? Does the NPC go back up and know to wait and then come back down?

"And I'm just scratching the surface of some of the problems they brought up. So, it seems simple, and other games have climbing ladders, but we chose to put our efforts into other things to make them better rather than deal with that. So, I'd like to see Bethesda finally come around to making ladders a reality where you're actually climbing them and make the world feel a little more immersive."

While we know very little about Sentinel right now - much less how it's going to solve the ladder problem -that hasn't stopped fans from speculating about a number of topics, including what they believe is going to be a split / alternate timeline setup.

#3857. "A fight for all workers": SAG-AFTRA throw weight behind emerging Rockstar union ahead of its GTA 6 release week vote

In what has come to feel like the dawn of the final day before Grand Theft Auto VI's release, one thing that Rockstar really don't want people to be aware of is the ongoing legal dispute between the Rockstar Games Workers Union and the studio itself following Rockstar's alleged union busting in firing 31 union members last year. Starting on the 12th through to the 26th, recognition of the union will be voted upon by staff to ensure that workers would be given a say over "topics including pay and bonuses, overtime, redundancies, flexible working arrangements, and generative AI policies."

If it passes, the vote would also make the union the largest recognised union in the UK games industry, partly thanks to its partnership with the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain. Now, the global labor union SAG-AFTRA have chimed in to endorse the Workers Union, offering solidarity to the members involved and granting important leverage from a global force.

SAG-AFTRA's statement declares that "unionisation is vital for the future of the video game industry", and that "in the face of record layoffs, job instability, hostile work places, and toxic crunch culture, it is now more critical than ever for unions and workers to stand in support of one another." They advocate for fair treatment, especially in the wake of displacement due to corporate mismanagement and genAI, and proudly state that "this is a fight for all workers."

Their statement closes by saying that "the gaming industry is a commercial juggernaut, and the people that create these amazing works of art deserve fair treatment and the opportunity to improve the terms of their employment with a strong voice at the bargaining table. We honor the courage of our fellow game workers at Rockstar and proudly support their union vote."

Solidarity with the workers, always. We can only wait and see how the voting process pans out.

#3856. Nintendo's legendary Kirby designer Masahiro Sakurai weighs in on gen-AI, saying "it has yet to gain my trust" but not to reject it completely

"Doing nothing is probably not the right approach."

Masahiro Sakurai, the designer behind many iconic Nintendo franchises such as Super Smash Bros. and several Kirby titles, has weighed in on the ongoing discussion of generative-AI use in game development.

At an event celebrating the release of his new book - Masahiro Sakurai’s Thoughts on Games - the veteran director told Famitsu he hasn't and currently isn't using the technology to make games, noting that the role of a designer is to generate ideas.

"It has yet to gain my trust," Sakurai said via DeepL machine translation. Regarding graphical use specifically, he added that, "It must not amount to exploitation of any kind," and that "for the time being, we can produce better results by coming up with ideas ourselves".

But Sakurai is wary of rejecting gen-AI completely, saying "making games today is far too difficult", with some games "running at a loss even after selling millions of copies". A company in that position may go under if it does not change its stance on generative-AI, he suggested. "Doing nothing is probably not the right approach," he said, but "where and how to use it" is a complex topic with a lot of uncertainties. Sakurai is taking "a slow-paced approach" for now.

Outside of regular industry layoffs, the use of generative-AI in games has been the most controversial topic amongst developers and players. Some argue it's already being used in multiple development disciplines, notably programming and writing code. Others, such as Shigeru Miyamoto, are more sceptical of the technology's capabilities, especially when it comes to the more creative and art-driven parts of game development.

World of Warcraft: Forever's been pretty great. At this point, I have around 150 hours played, a terrible posture problem, and a level 47 warrior I just barely avoided doing a 2 am Zul'Farrak run with yesterday. Speaking of, there has been a point of contention: Dungeons.

My position on the debate is fairly neutral—I think you could maybe bump up the mob XP by around 10% as a compromise—but overall I think they're fine. The new ones are bangers, and I get a huge bunch of XP from doing them at least once. Blizzard's recent choices, however, did have me scratching my head over the weekend.

For a short time, via a hotfix, enemies in dungeons wouldn't give experience points to anyone in the group if they were trivial (that is, greyed out) to at least one party member. On paper, this sounds incredibly reasonable. WoW has suffered from a plague of dungeon boosters (that is, people selling runs of dungeons to let folks AFK through their levelling journey) particularly in Classic.

But the moment you take a second to stare at how Classic dungeons are designed, you start to see the cracks form. Uldaman, for instance, has a level range of 41-51 in my dungeon finder. Maraudon, 46-55. Then there's the issue of the Scarlet Monastery, whose entire gauntlet runs from level 30 to 44 and is often done in one big sweep by groups.

In other words, it was possible to be maybe a couple levels over the recommended range for a dungeon—which is certainly a great help, but I don't think can be counted as a boost—and ruin the already-diminished XP gains for everyone. Which is counter-intuitive in a game that's meant to be social.

To Blizzard's credit, its devs did spring into action on Saturday, amending the hotfix: "Yesterday, we updated dungeon play so that experience granted by an enemy in an instance is nullified if a high level player is in the group and enemy is trivial to that player. For some dungeons, the new restriction missed the mark because of the overall level range of the enemies in the dungeon.

"With hotfixes that are now live, we’ve just deployed a further change to this restriction, making it so that the XP nullification only kicks in when the high-level player is more than 12 levels above the level of the enemies."

To me that's more than reasonable. I don't think, say, a level 25 character coming to help their mate out with Deadmines should be ruining the XP gains for everybody else—sure, their presence makes the dungeon a heck of a lot easier, but so does grouping up for quests in the open world. 12 levels seems a fair compromise.

#3854. In a reveal that might worry eventual PC players glancing at their GPUs, GTA 6 will target 30fps on all consoles

Oh, and and it'll be streamable on the Xbox One before it's playable on PC

In a press release coinciding with Grand Theft Auto VI becoming available for pre-load ahead of its November 19th release date, Rockstar has confirmed that the game "has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles, targeting 30 frames per second while pushing both platforms to their absolute limits." Read between the lines, and you can kind of make out the words "...so hope your PCs are up to spec, computer nerds."

GTA 6, of course, still does not have a confirmed PC version, even if Rockstar's former tech director says it's probably not far off. And despite this, even ancient, last-gen consoles are getting in on it, as the release also unexpectedly confirms that the game will be playable on Xbox One via Xbox Cloud Gaming, Microsoft's game streaming service that has suddenly lost its ability to work on PC. Granted, this comes with a warning: "as with all cloud streaming, connection speeds and other technical factors may influence game performance in ways that would not impact local gameplay." If you ended up getting a PS4 last generation, no cloud play for you either, I'm afraid. It also states that it will "play best on Playstation 5 consoles", making great use of that Sony partnership, and will include Playstation Spectral Super Resolution and ray-traced shadows on PS5 Pro.

A 2026 current-gen game targeting 30fps, let alone one as titanic of a release as GTA VI, is probably not going to go down well with a lot of people, even if console players are traditionally les sensitive about FPS counts than PC players. What this does imply, though, is that the inevitable PC release might be an even more demanding behemoth than expected, if Xbox Series and PS5 versions can't even target 60fps. The availability of the game on Xbox One, even if just through cloud streaming, could have resulted in an acceptance that 60fps just wasn't going to be possible if it was also going to be able to 'run' on last-gen hardware. Either way, when it does eventually escape console exclusivity, hopefully trying to run GTA VI on anything less than an RTX 5080 won't set your PC on fire. Now, let me just quickly have a glance at GPU prices. Oh, no.

#3853. Activision cracking down on popular Call of Duty: Warzone app that basically constituted cheating

"Lobby shopping" is what Call of Duty: Warzone players have been calling the ability to check the skill level of players in a lobby prior to joining it, enabling them to pass on those that include a lot of tough competition.

There are several ways players, notably Twitch streamers and content creators, have been able to do that over the years. But the use of one app in particular - Warzone Agent - has been considered by many to be cheating, and Activision is finally doing something about it.

Alongside the launch of Modern Warfare 4's version of Warzone and the game's first season of post-launch content, Call of Duty's anti-cheat team Ricochet has announced it's officially cracking down on Warzone Agent.

"Yesterday, we began taking action against Warzone Agent, a paid, unauthorised third party tool that lets users lobby shop in Warzone," the developer revealed in a post on X. "Ricochet anti-cheat will block players attempting to load the software and instruct them to unload it before accessing multiplayer."

Having the ability to cherrypick the lobby with the lowest-skilled players possible bypasses the game's matchmaking algorithm, potentially ruining the game for the dozens of other players in the match. Historically, content creators have used the app (and other methods) to post impressive kill records.

The developer added in a follow-up message that: "Using unauthorised software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision terms of use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement." The language seems to stop just short of outright confirming those players using Warzone Agent will be banned.

As part of this crackdown, Ricochet reiterated its stance on boosting - artificially increasing (or decreasing) one's skill rating - saying that it too is considered cheating. "Receiving a boost, having another player log in to boost your account, or purchasing a boosted account are all against policy," the developer said.

"Boosting services flood lobbies with low effort accounts used to farm XP and complete challenges. Those accounts can later be sold as Ranked Play ready, directly feeding the cheating marketplace."

More than 20,000 boosting-related accounts have been removed since the launch of Modern Warfare 4, according to the developer, and Ricochet will "continue to apply pressure" in this area.

The quality of multiplayer was a particular highlight in Eurogamer's review of Modern Warfare 4, in which Dom Peppiatt lauded the complexity of weapon handling, which works without taking away from accessibility of the gunplay.
